questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Correlation: Studying Relationships Between Variables' refers to.
questions.a: Summer heat brings crowds to hill stations and brisk ice-cream sales -- temperature, visitors and sales move together. Correlation is the statistical tool that studies such relationship: whether two variables move together, in which direction, and how closely.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Correlation: Studying Relationships Between Variables'.
questions.a: Do they move together, opposite, or not at all -- correlation answers the relationship question.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Correlation: Studying Relationships Between Variables' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: kest106.txt opening and types sections (temperature and ice cream example, meaning of correlation, positive negative and zero correlation))

concepts.title: Scatter Diagram and Karl Pearson's Coefficient

questions.q: Using the method 'Scatter Diagram and Karl Pearson's Coefficient', work with: cov_xy = 24, sd_x = 4, sd_y = 20. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of r_value.

Take the relation taught for 'Scatter Diagram and Karl Pearson's Coefficient' and work with: cov_xy = 100, sd_x = 25, sd_y = 5. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of r_value.
Explain in your own words what 'Scatter Diagram and Karl Pearson's Coefficient' refers to.
questions.a: A scatter diagram dots the pairs of values on a graph, giving a first visual verdict on relationship. Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation refines it to a precise number between -1 and +1, measuring both direction and degree of the linear relationship.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Scatter Diagram and Karl Pearson's Coefficient'.
questions.a: First the dots, then the number -- Pearson's r puts the scatter's message between -1 and +1.

concepts.title: Spearman's Rank Correlation and the Warning of Causation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Spearman's Rank Correlation and the Warning of Causation' refers to.
questions.a: When data are ranked rather than measured, Spearman's rank correlation compares the differences in ranks to obtain a coefficient. And a caution closes the chapter: high correlation does not prove causation -- a third factor or pure coincidence may drive both variables together.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Spearman's Rank Correlation and the Warning of Causation'.
questions.a: Ranks correlate too -- and even a perfect r is evidence of association, never proof of cause.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Spearman's Rank Correlation and the Warning of Causation' taught, and from which source text?
